full_judgment:
29. It can be, also, profitably observed that though sad, yet it is a fact that people do not hesitate in resorting to vengeance over the unfortunate death of their near and dear ones. There is a tendency to rope in as many people as possible for facing trial in respect of death or injury to unfortunate victim. It has been found that on occasions innocent persons including the aged, infirm ladies and children are booked for standing on the dock and remain confined in custody till pendency of cases. Some are acquitted by court of First instance and some by Appellate Court but only after languishing in confinement for years. Such efforts on the part of unscrupulous survivors of crime or relatives of the victim invariably but unfortunately help the real culprits as it becomes difficult on the part of Court/Tribunal to shift grain out of chaff. Under such circumstances and in view of prevalent Criminal Jurisprudential System in the country, the doctrine of presumption of innocence in favour of the accused makes Justice System itself a victim which ultimately weakens the Criminal Justice dispensation system. In cases of group clashes involving a number of persons as accused a balance approach by Court is required to be insisted so that neither an innocent person should be convicted nor a guilty person be acquitted. Every case in the final analysis would de-pend upon its own fact. 

 "The presumption against retrospective construction has no application to enactments which affect only the procedure and practice of the courts. No person has a vested right in any course of procedure. Alterations in the form of procedure are always retrospective unless there is some good reason or other way they should not be so." 

 "As a general rule, legislation which relates solely to procedure or to legal remedies will not be subject to the rule that statutes should not be given retrospective operation. Similarly, the presumption against retrospective construction is inapplicable. In other words, such statutes constitute an exception to the rule pertaining to statutes generally. Therefore, in the absence of a contrary legislative intention, statutes pertaining solely to procedure or legal remedy may affect a right of action no matter whether it come into existence prior to, or after the enactment of, the statute. Similarly, they may be held applicable to proceedings pending or subsequently commenced. In any event, they will, at least, presumptively apply to accrued and pending as well as to future actions."
